Photo: Iraqi PMO Show caption: Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi addresses the armed forces on Fr… Iraq's Ali Al Zaidi says Jurf Al Sakhar is start of state asserting control
 Tanks and armoured vehicles roll into area as government forces begin taking up positions under security agreement with Kataib Hezbollah
 Mina Aldroubi November 20, 2026
 Add on Google 
 Iraqi security forces entered Jurf Al Sakhar on Friday, deploying tanks and armoured vehicles to reassert state authority over the long-held militia stronghold.
 A compromise deal requires Kataib Hezbollah members to withdraw and relocate, with federal police and the Popular Mobilisation Forces assuming control of the area.
 A new joint security headquarters was established, uniting army, federal police, energy police and PMF units to oversee security and protect oil infrastructure.
 The operation marks Baghdad's most significant move in over a decade to bring armed groups under state control without triggering direct confrontation between Shiite factions.
 This step would "break the last stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah since the war on ISIS," said an Iraq expert at Crisis Group. 
 The Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi said the entry of security forces into Jurf Al Sakhar on Friday is the beginning of the assertion of state authority across the country, after troops entered the area controlled by the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia for more than a decade. 
 Tanks and armoured vehicles rolled into Jurf Al Sakhar as government forces began taking up positions under a security agreement with Kataib Hezbollah, marking Baghdad's most significant move in years to reassert authority over the area. 
 A compromise ​deal was established late on Thursday to ease tension ​with Iran's most powerful militia ally in the country. Under ​the ⁠deal, Kataib Hezbollah members were expected to withdraw to ⁠other ​parts of the ​country while federal police and the Popular Mobilisation Forces were set to take over parts of the area. 
 Headphones Beyond the Headlines What will come of Iraq’s Jurf Al Sakhar operation?
 Listen Now Arrow "It is the beginning of a unified, strong and just Iraq, governed by the constitution and the law," Mr Al Zaidi said in an address on Friday. 
 "Our decision is firm: no weapons outside the authority of the state, no weapons except Iraq’s weapons, no decision except Iraq’s decision, and no flag higher than Iraq’s flag," he added. Mr Al Zaidi has vowed to bring all weapons and non-state actors under the Iraqi state, with the situation in Jurf Al Sakhar proving to be a major test. 
 "From Jurf Al Sakhar, we begin asserting state authority across all of ​Iraq, confronting ⁠corruption and weapons beyond state control," he said. 
 Founded in the aftermath of the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, Kataib ​Hezbollah is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, the umbrella group of hardline Shiite armed organisations supported by Iran. 
 The militia quickly developed ​a reputation for deadly attacks against ‌military and diplomatic targets during the US-led counter-insurgency war and sectarian conflict of the 2000s, using snipers, rockets, mortars and roadside bombs. 
 Iraqi officers speak at the opening on Friday of a command headquarters to oversee security operations in the Jurf Al Sakhar area. Reuters Show caption: Iraqi officers speak at the opening on Friday of a command h… The government established a new joint security headquarters in the district south of Baghdad, bringing together units from the army, federal police, energy police and PMF. The command is tasked with overseeing security, protecting oil infrastructure and reopening key roads in the area. 
 “The deployment of forces and the handover of areas of responsibility are taking place starting today. The command headquarters has been granted full powers by Mr Al Zaidi to maintain security and enforce the law in the Jurf Al Nasr area,” government spokesman Sabah Al Numan said at a media conference on the outskirts of the area on Friday morning, using the name given to the area by the PMF after liberating it from ISIS. 
 The operation is a test of Baghdad's broader effort to bring armed groups under state control while avoiding a confrontation between competing Shiite groups. 
 Experts say the outcome in Jurf Al Sakhar could shape the government's wider campaign to curb the influence of militias and strengthen central authority across Iraq. 
 Iraqi soldiers in Jurf Al Sakhar. AFP Show caption: Iraqi soldiers in Jurf Al Sakhar. AFP "This is a significant change to the past 12 years, when the area was out of reach to the government. If it’s enforced as planned, it will break the last stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah since the war on ISIS," Lahib Hagel, an Iraq expert at Crisis Group, told The National . "But questions remain regarding the areas that will be controlled by the Hashd Brigades [PMF] and whether Kataib Hezbollah will be able to exercise influence through them." 
 Jurf Al Sakhar, about 60km south-west of Baghdad, has remained largely closed to civilians and the government for more than a decade. 
 The predominantly Sunni area was recaptured from ISIS in 2014 by the Kataib Hezbollah fighters alongside the Iraqi army, but most former residents have been barred from returning. Iraqi officials have increasingly linked the restoration of state authority in the district to plans for reopening the area and addressing the long-standing displacement issues.
